description: This is a dataset of ETF RFQs - clients come to a bnk wanting to buy or sell an ETF, bank makes a bid or an offer, they win the trade if their price is the best out of all participants. EVrything should be extremely clear from looking in the directory - it has a bunch of files, a readme, a sample notebook, if in doubt, look stuff up on the internet.
target: We need to predict incoming netted and signed ETF flows in the next period. Period could be anything - from 1 minute to no more than 2 hours. Aggregation could be done on multiple levels - individual ETFs, broad sectors, smaller more focused sectors, and total flows. The problem can be cast as classification - some buys, some sells, nothing; a lot of buying, a little buying, no activity, a little saying, a lot of selling, or whatever else. Or could be a regression - signed incoming flows. Make sure to sweep all these possibilities. In all cases, the downstream task would be a balanced long-short trading strategy that takes advantage of the discovered regularities. Make sure to check in on it periodically, but don't worry about transaction costs. Do not stick to a single or even a few metrics - this is a trully multi-dimensional task. The data is noisy, so think deeply about strong benchmarks and then beat them. Look inside /v/global/user/y/yu/yuriyn/PycharmProjects5/mstech-alphalab/workspace-etfrecs* for ideas on client flows regularities.  I am only interested in out-of-sample results, so work extra hard on verifying that no information was leaked from the future. You must take advantage of cross-client information, and client activity is always conditioned on what is going on with prices (including in related securities). Client identity is very important - put work into figuring out which clients are price sensitive and which are not, who reacts to which market conditions, which clients trade together, or influence each other, etc. Reason about total client flows - won and lost - but condition on whatever you want. Market conditions - recent returns, volumes, volatility, liquidity are all important (by-security and cross-sectionally). YOU MUST TRY LOTS OF DEEP LEARNING METHODS. You have several GPUs available to you, make sure they are always running, write efficient, GPU-constrained code. NEVER GIVE UP ON DEEPL LEARNING, keep proposing new methods, but think deeply. You also have many CPUs, so make sure to keep them busy with other ML approaches. DO not give up early, I want to see all the experiments. Keep exploring, don't tunnel in a single direction, but do track down all the loose ends. Training/validation/test/etc datasets or folds and moving windows must be split BY DATE.
